sammendrag: During the last three decades, concern about the skills of the U.S. workforce has emerged as a persistent public policy issue. In the late 1970s and early 1980s, sluggish U.S. labor productivity growth generated alarm over a perceived gap between the skills of U.S. workers and workers in other industrialized countries. In the 1990s, concerns arose about Americans being left behind as substantial changes in the labor market reduced the real earnings and labor force participation of lessskilled workers. The current focus on skills and their importance in the working lives of Americans is not new, rather a renewal. Federal training policy has its roots in New Deal public works programs. Today’s programs are the descendants of programs initiated during the Johnson Administration’s War on Poverty. Several factors can be tied to the renewed public interest in skill development.
